issues.subcategory: attempt window length contradiction
issues.description: The manuscript inconsistently defines the length of the suicide attempt episode. Multiple places state that analyses focused on the two weeks before an attempt, but the methods also define attempt episodes as the one-week period prior to the attempt. This discrepancy affects the core operationalization of the primary predictor, undermines interpretability of the time analyses, and makes replication difficult.
issues.quote: Abstract: "Mixed-effects models tested whether these constructs differed in general (means) and over time (slopes) two weeks before a suicide attempt"; Methods, Interview and episode identification: "Episodes included: 1) past actual, interrupted, or aborted suicide attempts, using the one-week period prior to the attempt as a ‘suicide attempt episode’"; Overview and Hypotheses: "two weeks preceding a suicide attempt"

issues.subcategory: incorrect significance value for sadness effect
issues.description: The p-value for the omnibus effect of episode type on sadness is reported inconsistently across sections and tables. In the Results text it is reported as p=.003, whereas Table 2 reports p=.033 for the same test statistic (χ²=8.74, df=3). These cannot both be correct and materially change the strength of evidence.
issues.quote: Results: "there was a significant effect of episode type on use of sad words, 2(3)=8.74, p=.003."; Table 2: "Sadness (sad) | 2=8.74 | 3 | 3 | .033"

issues.subcategory: discussion claims unsupported by results
issues.description: The Discussion states that mean-difference analyses showed greater anxiety and sadness before attempts, but the Results report no significant omnibus effect for anxiety. This overstates findings and may mislead readers about which results were actually supported.
issues.quote: Discussion: "results indicated that the period of high risk just before a suicide attempt was associated with messages indicating greater anxiety and sadness."; Table 2: "Anxiety (anx) | 2=3.62 | 3 | 3 | .306"

issues.subcategory: misreported chi-square notation/statistic
issues.description: Throughout the results tables and text, chi-square statistics are reported as "2(3)=..." rather than χ²(3)=..., suggesting formatting loss or statistical reporting error. While partly typographic, the manuscript repeatedly labels likelihood-ratio tests as "Likelihood-ratio (Wald chi-square) tests," conflating distinct test families. Likelihood-ratio tests and Wald tests are not interchangeable, and the ambiguity prevents correct interpretation of inferential procedures.
issues.quote: "Likelihood-ratio (Wald chi-square) tests were performed to compare goodness of fit for models including and excluding the fixed effect of episode type."; "there was a significant effect of episode type on use of sad words, 2(3)=8.74"

issues.subcategory: incorrect p-value range
issues.description: For death-word interaction follow-ups, the p-value range includes .067-.739, but one of the listed pairwise p-values in Table 3 is .412, making the stated range inaccurate. This indicates careless reporting of inferential results.
issues.quote: Results: "there were no significant differences in change over time for attempt compared to all other episodes (zs=0.33-1.83, ps=.067-.739)"; Table 3 includes p-values ".067", ".739", and ".412"

issues.subcategory: excessive precision/inconsistent p formatting
issues.description: One p-value is reported as .0111, inconsistent with the manuscript's general formatting and suggestive of transcription error or inadequate proofreading. Such discrepancies raise concern about reliability of the statistical reporting more broadly.
issues.quote: "positive (z=2.54, p=.0111) episodes"

issues.subcategory: retrospective episode identification with subjective dating
issues.description: The design relies on retrospective self-identification and dating of suicidal and non-suicidal episodes, sometimes from years earlier. Even if message content is objectively archived, the key exposure labels (attempt/ideation/depressed/positive episode and exact dates) are retrospective and vulnerable to recall bias and reconstruction. This is especially problematic for temporal slope analyses centered on day-level proximity to attempts.
issues.quote: "Individuals reporting a history of suicide attempt (N=33) retrospectively identified past attempts and periods of lower risk"; "participants were asked to identify a number of specific events or episodes in the past and the calendar dates during which the episodes took place"; "Participants were generally confident about the accuracy of the dates they selected"

issues.subcategory: heterogeneous and subjective attempt definition
issues.description: The primary high-risk category combines actual, interrupted, and aborted attempts, including incidents where no physical attempt was enacted and where participants themselves subjectively endorsed these as attempts. These are conceptually and clinically distinct phenomena with potentially different linguistic correlates. Collapsing them threatens construct validity of the 'suicide attempt' condition and may dilute or distort effects.
issues.quote: "attempt episodes (defined as actual, interrupted, and aborted attempts)"; "reported ‘suicide attempts’ also included incidents in which no physical attempt was enacted but in which participants considered their planning or actions to constitute a higher level of suicidal intent than ‘suicide ideation’ so they subjectively endorsed making an attempt on the screener questions."

issues.subcategory: mismatch between social engagement construct and measure
issues.description: The study operationalizes social engagement, thwarted belongingness, and burdensomeness using aggregate ratios of outgoing to incoming texts and message counts. These metrics do not validly capture perceived belongingness or burdensomeness, which are subjective interpersonal cognitions. Null findings are therefore difficult to interpret as tests of the interpersonal theory.
issues.quote: "In the current study, we tested whether suicide attempters demonstrated greater signs of disengagement from and burdensomeness on their social support networks prior to suicide attempts compared to other episodes by examining patterns in outgoing vs. incoming messages."

issues.subcategory: mismatch between self-focus and rumination
issues.description: The manuscript treats singular first-person pronoun use as an indicator of rumination/self-focus. Pronoun frequency is at best an indirect proxy and may reflect conversational style, grammar, or topic rather than maladaptive self-focused rumination. This weak operationalization limits conclusions about the psychological construct supposedly measured.
issues.quote: "we tested whether use of first-person pronouns (as an indicator of rumination) was greater prior to suicide attempts"

issues.subcategory: positive mood versus typical mood inconsistency
issues.description: The manuscript alternates between describing the low-risk comparison episode as 'positive mood' and 'typical mood (i.e., neither particularly positive nor negative mood).' These are not equivalent constructs. Inconsistent operationalization of the comparison condition undermines interpretation of episode contrasts.
issues.quote: Introduction: "periods of lower risk (e.g., suicide ideation only or depressed mood)" and later "depressed/positive mood"; Methods: "4) two-week episode of typical mood (i.e., neither particularly positive nor negative mood and no ideation or attempt)."; Results/Table labels use "positive mood" and "positive episodes."

issues.subcategory: causal language from retrospective observational data
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly suggests that text features can identify suicide risk in real time and that communication markers may predict imminent risk. But the design is retrospective, observational, and based on post hoc labeling of past episodes; no real-time prediction or prospective validation occurred. Such causal/predictive framing overstates what can be inferred.
issues.quote: Title: "Can Text Messages Identify Suicide Risk in Real Time?"; Abstract: "Results suggest private electronic communication has the potential to provide real-time digital markers of suicide risk."; Introduction: "we aimed to improve our ability to assess suicide risk dynamically in real time."

issues.subcategory: post hoc selection of time window
issues.description: The manuscript states the two-week window was chosen conservatively, but also says the optimal window was empirically assessed using visual inspection of smoothed plots to identify when change appeared most pronounced. This introduces substantial researcher degrees of freedom in defining the analytic window after looking at the data, which can bias effect estimates and p-values if not clearly separated from confirmatory analyses.
issues.quote: "The decision to set each episode at two weeks long was made in a conservative effort... The question of the optimal time window was also assessed empirically, using visual inspection of descriptive figures to identify when the rate of change appeared to be most pronounced."

issues.subcategory: no preregistration despite a priori claim
issues.description: The manuscript says selected features were tested 'a priori,' yet no preregistration or timestamped analysis plan is described. Given multiple constructs, outcomes, episode definitions, data subsets, and supplementary robustness checks, lack of preregistration raises concern about selective reporting and analytical flexibility.
issues.quote: "We analyzed and compared text messages during episodes within person based on a number of features selected a priori"; no preregistration is described anywhere in the manuscript.

issues.subcategory: multiple testing without correction
issues.description: The study runs a large number of omnibus and pairwise tests across many outcomes and two primary analyses, yet explicitly declines multiple-comparisons correction. In a small pilot with exploratory elements, this materially elevates false-positive risk, especially for marginal findings such as p=.049 and p=.046.
issues.quote: "our analyses involved running a fairly large number of tests... we decided not to artificially suppress Type I error (i.e., using a multiple comparisons correction)"

issues.subcategory: selection bias from requiring recoverable SMS archives
issues.description: Eligibility required participants to have accessible historical messaging data dating back before attempts, and many episodes were missing because old devices/cloud backups were unavailable. This likely selects for specific phone usage/storage behaviors and excludes many relevant episodes or people, biasing the sample in ways not fully characterized.
issues.quote: "participants were excluded if they did not have access to at least one data service type... dating back to before their most recent suicide attempt"; "efforts to collection additional messages outside of their current mobile device were minimally successful"; "Among the episodes queried during the lab interview, 134 (46%) episodes contained SMS data"

issues.subcategory: substantial episode-level missingness not formally addressed
issues.description: Less than half of identified episodes had SMS data, and only 27 of 33 participants contributed analyzable episode data. The manuscript treats this as a mixed-model advantage but does not evaluate whether missingness was associated with episode type, recency, phone platform, or participant characteristics. If missingness is informative, estimates may be biased.
issues.quote: "A total of 293 episodes were collected... Among the episodes queried during the lab interview, 134 (46%) episodes contained SMS data, collected from 27 different participants."; "Using mixed models allowed us to ... handle missing data"

issues.subcategory: missing not at random assumptions untested
issues.description: The claim that mixed models 'handle missing data' is too broad. Mixed models generally require assumptions such as missing at random conditional on modeled variables. Here, missingness likely depended on device changes, backup settings, episode recency, and perhaps episode severity. These mechanisms were not modeled or tested, so missing data could bias results.
issues.quote: "A mixed-effects method was selected because of its well-established advantages in terms of... ability to handle missing data"

issues.subcategory: excluding currently high-risk individuals
issues.description: Participants with high or imminent current suicide risk were excluded. While ethically understandable, this means the sample may underrepresent individuals most likely to show acute risk markers, limiting the relevance of findings to imminent-risk assessment.
issues.quote: "Any participants with intense thoughts of suicide who were determined to be at 'high risk' or 'imminent risk' for suicidal behavior... were excluded from study participation"

issues.subcategory: narrow sample demographics
issues.description: The sample was predominantly female, White, college-aged, and recruited largely from a university/community context. This sharply limits generalizability to older adults, males, more racially diverse populations, clinical populations, and those at highest lethality risk.
issues.quote: "Most of the participants were female, White, and college-aged."; Table 1: "Mean (SD) age in years | 20.4 (2.4)" and "Sex (% female) | 84.8"

issues.subcategory: nonlethal and largely non-enacted attempt sample
issues.description: The study's high-risk episodes are mostly nonfatal, often non-enacted, and 71% involved no physical harm. Findings may not generalize to medically serious attempts or suicide deaths, yet the paper sometimes discusses suicide risk broadly. Linguistic patterns for aborted/interrupted acts may differ from those preceding lethal attempts.
issues.quote: "71% of incidents did not result in any physical harm"; "logistics of accessing and downloading communication data necessitated enrolling participants with non-lethal attempts"

issues.subcategory: episode non-independence and overlap unclear
issues.description: Participants could contribute up to three episodes per type, but the manuscript does not specify whether episodes overlapped in time, how repeated attempts close together were handled, or whether the same messages could belong to more than one episode. Without clear rules, within-subject comparisons and random-effects structure are difficult to assess.
issues.quote: "A total of 3 to 12 episodes were collected for each participant"; "For each episode type, we asked about a maximum of three episodes"

issues.subcategory: insufficient details on episode classification procedures
issues.description: The manuscript says additional questions were used to minimize misclassification and references Supplement 1, but does not provide the actual criteria, thresholds, or decision rules used to classify episodes as ideation, depressed, typical/positive, interrupted, or aborted attempt. Replication and validity assessment are therefore limited.
issues.quote: "Participants answered additional questions about each reported episode as a way to minimize the risk of misclassification... Additional descriptive characteristics are available as Supplement 1 online."

issues.subcategory: no details on model convergence/singularity diagnostics
issues.description: Given the complex random-effects structures and small number of participants, convergence and singular-fit problems are likely. The manuscript notes some models did not converge but provides no diagnostics, optimizer settings, singularity checks, or whether final models were stable, limiting confidence in estimates.
issues.quote: "Models with the full set of random slopes did not converge; therefore, no random slopes were included in the final model."

issues.subcategory: problematic random effects specification including message intercept
issues.description: The manuscript describes random intercepts for participant, episode, and message while analyzing at the message level. A random intercept for each message is not meaningful if each row is a unique message observed once; it would absorb residual variance and is generally unidentified/useless. This suggests confusion about the model structure actually fit.
issues.quote: "a maximal random effects model, which included random intercepts of participant, episode, and message"; "A random by-participant slope for episode type and random intercepts of participant, participant-episode, and message were included"

issues.subcategory: day variable miscoded/ambiguously coded as factor
issues.description: The time variable is described as a 'numerical factor ranging from -14 to 0.' A variable cannot simultaneously be a numeric linear term and a factor in the usual modeling sense. If treated as a factor, slope interpretations and linear interaction claims are inappropriate; if numeric, the wording is wrong. This ambiguity directly affects the meaning of 'change over time.'
issues.quote: "day of episode (numerical factor ranging from -14 to 0)"

issues.subcategory: inappropriate/unclear power analysis for mixed models
issues.description: The power analysis appears disconnected from the actual hierarchical GLMM design. It references Cramer's V for chi-square tests, a 'design effect,' and assumes 60 attempts but only 20 with usable SMS data, despite the final analysis involving messages nested in episodes nested in participants and 21 attempts with SMS data. This does not transparently justify sample size for the planned mixed-effects analyses.
issues.quote: "We determined that a sample size of 30 suicide attempters (representing 60 attempts but only 20 with collected, usable SMS data, divided by the design effect) would provide enough power to detect only large effect sizes (Cramer’s V=0.29) for chi-square tests of mixed-effects models"

issues.subcategory: effect size reporting inaccurate
issues.description: The manuscript states that standardized β values in log-odds units serve as effect sizes. Log-odds coefficients are not standardized effect sizes unless explicitly standardized, and even then interpretation differs from conventional effect size metrics. This is misleading for readers trying to assess magnitude.
issues.quote: "Here, β (standardized values of the model parameter estimates in log odds units) are reported and serve as effect sizes."

issues.subcategory: ignoring recipient/context heterogeneity
issues.description: Message-level analyses pool texts across all recipients and contexts, though language differs substantially by recipient (romantic partner, parent, peer), group-vs-individual threads, and situational context. Without modeling recipient or conversation thread, observed differences may reflect changes in who participants texted rather than suicide risk per se.
issues.quote: "all available SMS data from each device were downloaded (i.e., not from only certain dates or recipients)"

issues.subcategory: unaddressed time-varying confounds
issues.description: Temporal changes in language before attempts may be driven by unmeasured time-varying factors such as relationship conflict, exams, sleep deprivation, alcohol/drug use, treatment changes, or life events. Because episodes were selected based on broad affective states and not matched on context, attributing differences specifically to suicide risk is unwarranted.
issues.quote: "participants were then asked to describe specific details of and context surrounding each time period" but these contextual variables were not incorporated into the models.

issues.subcategory: LIWC limitations acknowledged but central claims persist
issues.description: The study relies on LIWC single-word categories despite recognizing that negation and semantic context are not captured. Because key conclusions hinge on emotional-word trends, this measurement limitation directly threatens validity of the observed 'positive emotion' and 'anger' signals.
issues.quote: "One weakness of this approach is that examining single words in isolation can fail to capture the semantic context of the word (e.g., 'not happy' would count as 'positive emotion' because negation is not accounted for)"

issues.subcategory: insufficient data cleaning and preprocessing detail
issues.description: The manuscript says SMS files were individually cleaned using Python and LIWC percentages were converted to counts, but does not provide code details, tokenization rules, treatment of emojis, URLs, attachments, duplicated messages across backups, group texts, non-English text, or message normalization. These omissions hinder reproducibility and validity assessment.
issues.quote: "participants’ SMS data files were individually cleaned using Python to standardize the encoding of messages and naming of variables"; "LIWC percentage scores were converted into counts"

issues.subcategory: no descriptive distribution of messages across episode types
issues.description: The paper reports total messages and broad average per episode, but not the number of messages/episodes per episode type, per participant, or per day. Uneven data density across conditions could strongly affect mixed-model estimates and power, especially for slope analyses.
issues.quote: "Across all episodes, 189,478 text messages were collected and analyzed, ranging between on average about 1,200-1,600 text messages per episode."

issues.subcategory: possible denominator issue for proportion modeling
issues.description: The methods say LIWC percentage scores were converted to counts and entered as proportions, but it is not specified what denominator was used for each message or how zero-word/very short messages were handled. Many SMS messages are extremely short; proportion models can be unstable or undefined for empty or one-word messages, affecting validity.
issues.quote: "These LIWC percentage scores were converted into counts and then entered as proportions in our models (i.e., number of words in a given text message belonging to versus not belonging to the LIWC category)"

issues.subcategory: short-message granularity problem
issues.description: SMS messages are often fragmented across multiple consecutive texts. Treating each message as an independent observation may split a single utterance into several units, distorting LIWC proportions and inflating sample size without corresponding informational gain. Conversation-level aggregation or thread-level modeling may have been more appropriate.
issues.quote: "This approach also allowed us to maximize sources of variance by analyzing on the message level rather than only mean values by episode"

issues.subcategory: participant pool versus community recruitment ambiguity
issues.description: The manuscript says participants were recruited from the Charlottesville community, yet the screening procedure appears based on a participant pool pretest administered at the beginning of a semester, implying heavy university-student recruitment. This ambiguity matters for understanding the sample frame and external validity.
issues.quote: "A sample of 33 participants... were recruited from the Charlottesville community."; "Participant pool participants were selected based on two surveys... On the participant pool pretest administered at the beginning of the semester"

issues.subcategory: mislabeling digital biomarkers/phenotyping claims
issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly refers to LIWC-derived text features as 'digital biomarkers' or phenotyping indicators of suicide risk. Biomarker language implies stronger specificity, validity, and often biological grounding than is established here. Given retrospective labeling, weak construct validity for some measures, and no prospective validation, this terminology is overstated.
issues.quote: "possible novel, real-time digital biomarkers of suicidal behaviors"; "private electronic communication from past suicide attempters as a potential source of real-time digital biomarkers of heightened suicide risk"

issues.subcategory: platform- and era-specific communication behavior
issues.description: Findings from SMS archives in a young sample may not generalize to current communication ecosystems where messaging occurs through encrypted or proprietary apps (e.g., Snapchat, WhatsApp, Instagram DM). Since communication medium shapes language and metadata, the applicability of SMS-based markers is limited.
issues.quote: "it should be acknowledged... data collection of SMS and other private digital communication is likely to remain an ongoing challenge... as younger populations transition to closed ecosystems and proprietary platforms (e.g., Snapchat)"

issues.subcategory: missing control for language/sample exclusions
issues.description: The manuscript does not report whether non-English messages were excluded, whether participants had to be English-speaking, or how multilingual texting was handled. LIWC dictionaries are language-specific; including unmatched language data would bias scores.
issues.quote: No explicit statement is provided on language inclusion/exclusion, despite use of LIWC2015 dictionaries on SMS content.

issues.subcategory: no blinding in episode identification/interview
issues.description: The experimenter both assisted with data download and conducted retrospective episode interviews. There is no indication of blinding during coding or analysis stages. Although message scoring was automated, episode labeling—the key predictor—was vulnerable to interviewer expectancy effects and participant demand characteristics.
issues.quote: "participants were interviewed by the experimenter and asked to identify a number of episodes"
